title: Feedback both ways
gist: Asher asks Maya to push back earlier and more visibly in planning, with numbers; Maya tells Asher he says yes to too many stakeholders, and his 'let's see if we can fit it' reads as a commitment, which he admits is likely how Tom heard live ETA.

turns.t: Okay. Can I give you some feedback? It's kind of related.
Yeah. Go.

So, I think part of how we end up here is, in planning, you tend to raise capacity concerns late, and kind of quietly. Like, I've seen you in the room, you'll say something like, 'that might be tight,' and then afterward, in a one-on-one, I hear 'that's actually impossible.' And by then it's committed and everyone's moved on. I'd love for you to push back earlier and more visibly. In the room. With numbers. Because when you say 'it's tight,' Tom hears 'it's doable.' When you say 'we have eleven engineers, here's what's committed, here's the five weeks this costs, here's what it pushes out,' nobody can argue with that.
Hm.

And I want to say, it's not that you're wrong. You're usually right. It's that the room doesn't get the benefit of it in time to do anything about it. Like, Q3 planning, the dispatcher bulk-edit thing. You said 'that's going to be tight' in the meeting, and then two weeks later it was the reason the beta slipped from August to September. If you'd put a number on it in the room, I think we'd have just not done it.

No, that's fair. That's, yeah. Bulk edit is a good example, I knew it was three weeks and I said 'tight.' I think I do soften it. Part of it is I don't want to be the person who always says no. Like, eng is always the no. Eng is the department of no. I don't love being that, and I think I overcorrect.

I get that. But numbers aren't no. Numbers are just, here's the cost. Then the room decides. If you show up with the table, you're not saying no, you're making the tradeoff visible, and then it's everyone's decision, not yours.
Yeah. Okay. Actually, that's helpful framing. I'm going to steal that. Okay, can I give you some back?
Please. Yes.

So, I think the other half of how we end up here is you say yes to too many stakeholders. And I don't mean, like, big yeses. I mean small ones. Tom asks for something in Slack, you say 'yeah, let's see if we can fit it.' Sofia asks for something for Brightside, 'yeah, we'll figure it out.' Leah wants a launch date for v3 for a campaign, 'yeah, that sounds right.' And each one's small, but they all land on my team, and they add up. And then I'm the one who has to go back and say actually, we can't. Which makes me the no person. Which is, you know, the thing I just said I don't want to be.
Oof. Yeah.
And I think 'let's see if we can fit it' sounds like a maybe to you, but to them it's a yes. Like, Tom probably thinks you agreed live ETA was coming. I don't know that, but I'd bet on it.

No. That's, you're probably right. I think he asked me about it a few weeks ago, in passing, and I said something like 'yeah, it's high on the list.' Which, to me, meant it's a candidate. To him, apparently, that's a roadmap commitment he can put in front of a customer. And then he's been carrying that around for three weeks, and from where he sits, product said yes, so why would he check with eng?
Right.

Okay. That's really fair, and honestly that one stings a bit because it's true. I think I do it because I hate being the bottleneck. Someone asks, I want to unblock them, and 'let's see' feels like the nice answer. But it's not nice if it turns into a surprise for your team three weeks later. So, I'm going to try to route stuff through planning instead of saying yes in Slack. And when I'm not sure, actually say 'I'm not sure, let me check with Maya,' instead of 'let's see.' And you can call me on it when I slip.
I will call you on it. Fair warning.
I know you will. Good. That's what I want. Honestly, if we both do our half, the Tom thing mostly doesn't happen.
Yeah. I think that's right. It's a two-sided leak. Sales hears a maybe as a yes, and engineering says tight when it means no. If we fix both ends, there's a lot less to clean up in the middle.

title: Growth toward Director, hiring loop, and commitments
gist: Maya wants to grow toward Director and will own the frontend hiring loop; Sam Rivera is a strong candidate heading to Asher's final round. They close on commitments: Asher talks to Tom and gets Daniel to take Monday off, and Maya brings a capacity model to Q4 planning.

turns.t: Okay, we've got, what, eight minutes. I wanted to make sure we actually talk about you this time. Last time you said you'd been thinking about what's next, and then we spent the whole hour on the outage.

Yeah. So, I've thought about it more. I want to grow toward Director. Not right now, I know we're sixty people, I know that's not a role that exists today. But I want to be working toward it, and I want the next year to build the stuff that gets me there. Like, owning more than just routing. Hiring, cross-team planning, that kind of thing. I've been an EM for almost three years now, and I think I'm good at running one team. What I haven't done is the stuff that's across teams, like, setting how we plan, how we hire, how platform and apps and ML fit together. And I think if I don't start practicing that now, then when the company is big enough to need a Director, someone from outside walks in and does it, and I'm kind of annoyed that I didn't go for it.

I think that's a great goal, and honestly I think you're closer than you think. The feedback I just gave you is actually part of it. Directors are the ones who make tradeoffs visible in the room. And, the capacity model thing, if that becomes the way we plan across all of engineering, not just your team, that's a Director-shaped thing. And I'd rather grow that from inside than hire it. So let's be deliberate. I can put together, like, a short list of what I'd expect a Director here to own in a year, and we can use it to pick the next couple of stretch things for you. Hiring's an obvious one.
Ha. Yeah, I heard that. I'd like that, actually.
What would be the concrete next step, from your side?

So, the concrete one, I want to own the frontend hiring loop. We're hiring the two senior frontend engineers, and right now it's kind of shared between me and Hannah and Priya, and nobody really owns it. I want to own it. Design the loop, calibrate the interviewers, own the bar, and make the hire or no-hire call with everyone's input. Right now different interviewers are asking totally different questions, and I think we're getting noisy signal. I want a written rubric, a real work-sample question instead of whiteboard trivia, the same design problem for every candidate so we can compare, and debriefs within twenty-four hours so we don't lose people. We're slow right now and good candidates have other offers.
Yes. Done. That's yours. I'll tell Hannah so it's clear she's partnering with you on it and you're the owner.

Thank you. And actually it's already going well. Sam Rivera, the candidate in Lisbon, Priya and I did the technical round on Monday, and they were really strong. Offline sync, really deep, like, the real stuff, not blog-post stuff. Great story about pushing back on a designer with data. The concerns are geospatial experience, which is thin, and about four hours of time zone overlap. But we recommended them for the final with you. And I think it was the first loop where Priya and I were scoring on the same rubric, more or less, and you could feel the difference. The debrief took five minutes because we'd seen the same things.

Yeah, Hannah put them on my calendar for next Tuesday. Anything specific you want me to dig into? And, to your point about speed, I'd like the decision within a day of that, so if we want them, we move fast. Can you and Hannah have an offer range ready going in, so we're not waiting on comp?

The maps stuff, and how they'd actually work with four hours of overlap. Like, how do they handle a fire at three p.m. our time when they've been offline for two hours. And yes on the offer range, I'll sort it with Hannah. I think if we wait a week we lose them, they mentioned they're talking to at least one other company.

Got it. Okay, let's wrap with commitments so we both leave with the same list. Me, I'll talk to Tom before planning tomorrow about live ETA. I'll make sure Daniel takes Monday off. I'll post something about the outage response to the team. And I'll tell Hannah you own the frontend loop.

And me, I'll bring a capacity model to Q4 planning. Eleven engineers, a table of weeks by project, v3 GA, onboarding, live ETA, the outage follow-ups, so everyone can see where the weeks go and what moves if we add live ETA. And I'll send you the per-fleet beta numbers today. I'll put the live ETA option in there both ways, the full five-week version and whatever the thinner version looks like if Daniel and I can scope it in time, so the room can actually choose.
Perfect. And in planning, put the table up early. Like, first ten minutes, before anyone's attached to anything.
First ten minutes. Got it.
Okay. Thanks, Maya. Seriously. This was a good one.
Yeah, it was. Thanks. Go talk to Tom.
Going. Well, tomorrow. Bye.
